pos: n. (chief city of Transylvania, Romanian Cluj; where the antitrinitarians took the city under Ferenc David)
etymology: From Hungarian Kolozsvar, the castle of Klaus; Romanian Cluj, German Klausenburg.
biblical_def: Kolozsvar was the largest city of Transylvania and it moved through three confessions in twenty years. Lutheran in the 1540s, Reformed in the 1550s, it then followed its own preacher Ferenc David, who had been Reformed superintendent, into the denial of the Trinity; by 1568 the city was the capital of the Hungarian Unitarian church, which it remained. David was condemned at last for denying that Christ should be prayed to, and died in prison in 1579. The Reformed kept a college in the city and the Unitarians kept another. The dictionary records Kolozsvar because its history shows how far a movement can travel when each step is taken by the same logic as the last. The doctrine the city abandoned is written on the face of the Gospels: at the Jordan the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends upon Him, and the Father speaks from heaven. “he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him” (Mat 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Spirit in theology as the Third Person of the Trinity; the dove as, in Scripture, a symbol of the Holy Spirit; and blasphemy as reproachful or irreverent words uttered impiously against Jehovah.
webster_full: SPIRIT, n. [L. spiritus.] In theology, the Third Person of the Trinity, the Holy Spirit; the divine agent of regeneration, conviction, sanctification, and the new birth.
DOVE, n. A fowl of the order Columbæ, the genus Columba. In scripture, a symbol of peace, of the Holy Spirit, and of the meek and innocent disposition.
BLASPHEMY, n. An indignity offered to God by words or writing; reproachful, contemptuous or irreverent words uttered impiously against Jehovah.
TRIN'ITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead.
scriptures: Mat 3:16
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
Mat 3:17
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
Act 5:4
Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
corruption_summary: Transylvania's chief city, Lutheran then Reformed then Unitarian under Ferenc David, who died in prison in 1579.
corruption_paragraphs: Unitarianism is the live corruption, and Kolozsvar is where it first became a state-recognised church. Its modern form has gone further than David did, abandoning the authority of Scripture altogether; but the step that mattered was his, and it was taken by men who had been Reformed superintendents and who believed they were purifying the faith of scholastic accretions.

The principle to recover is that the three Persons are revealed together, acting distinctly, in the plainest narratives of the Gospels. At the baptism all three are present: “he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him” (Mat 3:16), and the Father's voice follows, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mat 3:17). The apostolic benediction names all three as one source of blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost” (2Co 13:14). And the Spirit lied to is identified as God: “thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God” (Act 5:4).

pos: n. (princely capital of Transylvania, Romanian Alba Iulia; Gabriel Bethlen's academy of 1622)
etymology: From Hungarian Gyulafehervar, Gyula's white castle; Romanian Alba Iulia.
biblical_def: Gyulafehervar was the seat of the princes of Transylvania, and under Gabriel Bethlen it became for twenty years one of the best-endowed Reformed centres in Europe. Bethlen founded an academy there in 1622 and paid western salaries to bring in western professors: Johann Heinrich Alsted the encyclopaedist, Johann Heinrich Bisterfeld and Ludwig Philipp Piscator all came from Herborn and taught in a Transylvanian hill town. The prince also paid for a complete Hungarian Bible and for the education of Romanian clergy in the Reformed faith. The academy was wrecked by the Tatar raid of 1658 and moved. The dictionary records Gyulafehervar because a ruler who spends public money on teaching the law of God is doing what the Chronicler commends in Jehoshaphat, and the measure is the teaching, not the endowment. “they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prince as the chief of a body of men, the ruler of a tribe or people; instruction as the act of teaching or informing the understanding; and a college as a society of persons engaged in common pursuits.
webster_full: PRINCE, n. The chief of a body of men; the ruler of a tribe or people.
INSTRUC'TION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; information; the act of communicating knowledge.
COL'LEGE, n. A collection or assemblage; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits. An edifice appropriated to the use of students.
LAW, n. In Scripture, the Mosaic institutions, or the revealed will of God; the rule of moral conduct.
scriptures: And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
Ezr 7:10
For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
Mal 2:6
The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found in his lips: he walked with me in peace and equity, and did turn many away from iniquity.
And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
corruption_summary: Bethlen's academy of 1622, staffed from Herborn, with a Hungarian Bible and Romanian clergy at the prince's charge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measuring of a Christian institution by its funding and its faculty rather than by what is actually taught in it. Bethlen bought the best professors in Europe; what made the academy worth founding was that they taught the Scriptures, and the Tatars could burn the buildings without touching that.

The principle to recover is that systematic teaching of God's law to a whole people is the work a godly ruler supports. Jehoshaphat's commission is the model, and the book goes with the teachers: “they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah” (2Ch 17:9). The teacher's own preparation comes first: “Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel” (Ezr 7:10). The standard for the man is character with doctrine: “The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found in his lips” (Mal 2:6). And the work takes time in one place: Paul “continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them” (Act 18:11).

pos: n. (Hungarian town on the Bodrog; its Reformed college, founded 1531, where Comenius taught)
etymology: From Hungarian Sarospatak, the muddy stream, from saros and patak.
biblical_def: Sarospatak has kept a Reformed college since 1531, which makes it one of the oldest continuously taught Protestant schools in the world; Hungarians call it simply the Athens on the Bodrog. The Rakoczi family endowed it, its library became one of the great collections of central Europe, and from 1650 to 1654 John Amos Comenius taught there at the invitation of Susanna Lorantffy and wrote his school plan and his Latin schoolbooks for its classes. The college was dispersed under the Counter-Reformation, re-established, suppressed again under communism and restored in 1990. The dictionary records Sarospatak because an institution that has taught the Scriptures for five centuries in one town is a rarer thing than a famous reformer, and the aim of such a place is stated by the prophet. “The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary” (Isa 50:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a society of persons engaged in common pursuits and an edifice appropriated to the use of students, instruction as the act of teaching, and a generation as a single succession in natural descent.
webster_full: COL'LEGE, n. A collection or assemblage; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits. An edifice appropriated to the use of students.
INSTRUC'TION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; information; the act of communicating knowledge.
GENERATION, n. A single succession in natural descent, as the children of the same parents.
LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution.
scriptures: Isa 50:4

The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned.
Pro 4:13
Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her; for she is thy life.
Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come.
Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:
corruption_summary: A Reformed college kept in one town since 1531, endowed by the Rakoczis, where Comenius taught from 1650.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern preference for new institutions over old ones, on the assumption that an old school is necessarily a tired one. Sarospatak has been closed twice by hostile governments and reopened twice, and its continuity is the whole of its usefulness.

The principle to recover is that teaching aims at a timely word to a weary hearer, and that it is handed down across generations deliberately. The prophet names both the gift and its purpose: “The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary” (Isa 50:4). What is received must be gripped: “Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her; for she is thy life” (Pro 4:13). The old man's prayer is for time to hand it on: “until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come” (Psa 71:18). And the words must first be lodged where they cannot be taken: “these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6).

pos: n. (Hungarian city and fortress, Romanian Oradea; where the Varad Bible was being printed when the Turks took the town in 1660)
etymology: From Hungarian Nagyvarad, the great fortress, from nagy and varad; Romanian Oradea.
biblical_def: Nagyvarad was the eastern bulwark of Hungary and a Reformed city with a college and a press. In 1657 the press began a revised Hungarian Bible, prepared by Mihaly Szenci Kertesz; in August 1660 the Turks took the fortress after a six-week siege, and the printers carried the unfinished sheets out of the town, finishing the work at Kolozsvar in 1661 so that the volume is known both as the Varad Bible and the Hungarian Bible of the exile. The dictionary records Nagyvarad because the printers' decision is the entry's whole point: with the city falling, the thing judged worth carrying out was the Bible in the press. “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down” (Neh 6:3) is the right answer to every interruption that is not an emergency, and finishing is what Scripture commends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines work as effort, labour, employment; to finish as to arrive at the end of in performance, to complete; and a course as an order of succession, a series of appointed turns.
webster_full: WORK, n. Effort; labour; employment.
FINISH, v.t. To arrive at the end of, in performance; to complete; to bring to an end.
COURSE, n. Order of succession; a series of appointed turns, as of priests or soldiers on duty.
PARCHMENT, n. The skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing.
scriptures: Neh 6:3
And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?
Neh 6:15
So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Joh 17:4
I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.
corruption_summary: The press that began the Varad Bible in 1657, carried the sheets out when the Turks took the fortress in 1660, and finished at Kolozsvar.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of leaving good work unfinished because circumstances changed — the commentary abandoned, the translation shelved, the project dropped when the funding or the attention moved. Men under siege finished a Bible; a change of plan is not usually a siege.

The principle to recover is that a work given by God is to be carried through, and that completion is itself commended. Nehemiah's refusal is the model answer: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it” (Neh 6:3). The record notes the finishing and the time it took: “So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days” (Neh 6:15). Paul's summary of a life is a completed course: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). And the Lord's own report to the Father is the same word: “I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do” (Joh 17:4).

pos: n. (city of Upper Hungary, Slovak Kosice; where the diets of Bocskai and Bethlen confirmed Protestant liberties)
etymology: From Hungarian Kassa, of uncertain origin; Slovak Kosice, German Kaschau.
biblical_def: Kassa was the chief city of Upper Hungary and the place where Hungarian Protestantism won its legal standing. Stephen Bocskai made it his seat during the rising of 1604 to 1606 that produced the Peace of Vienna, the first imperial guarantee of Protestant worship in Hungary; Gabriel Bethlen held diets there; and the city's cathedral passed back and forth between the confessions as the balance shifted. Those liberties were real, repeatedly confirmed, and repeatedly narrowed, and the Hungarian Protestants spent the seventeenth century defending a charter rather than simply preaching. The dictionary records Kassa because legal liberty is a genuine mercy and a standing temptation: a church that has secured its freedom must still be asked what it is doing with it. “ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh” (Gal 5:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint and the power of acting as one thinks fit, free as being at liberty and not under restraint, and toleration as the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
webster_full: LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit.
FREE, a. Being at liberty; not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral.
TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.
scriptures: Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
Jam 1:25
But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.
All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not.
corruption_summary: Bocskai's seat and Bethlen's diets, where Hungarian Protestant worship was first guaranteed by imperial peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern reading of Christian liberty as the right to do as one pleases in matters God has not expressly forbidden, which is precisely the construction Paul forecloses. The Hungarian churches won a liberty of worship; the question Scripture puts to them and to us is what the liberty is for.

The principle to recover is that liberty is freedom to serve and never a licence for the flesh. Paul states the calling and the limit in one sentence: “ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13). Peter puts the two together as a paradox that is not one: “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God” (1Pe 2:16). James calls the law itself the law of liberty and makes doing the test: “whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed” (Jam 1:25). And lawful is not the same as wise: “All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient” (1Co 10:23).

pos: n. (Transylvanian town, Hungarian Nagyenyed, Romanian Aiud; the Bethlen College and the massacre of 1704)
etymology: From Hungarian Enyed, of uncertain sense; Romanian Aiud.
biblical_def: Enyed received the Bethlen College when the academy was moved from Gyulafehervar after the Tatar raid, and the school became the chief Reformed seminary of Transylvania. On the thirteenth of March 1704, during the Rakoczi war, imperial irregulars sacked the town; the college was burned, its library destroyed, and the professors and students who had stayed to defend the books were killed in the streets and in the building. The college was rebuilt and still stands. The dictionary records Enyed because the killing of a school's children is one of the things Scripture refuses to explain away, and it supplies the words for grieving it rather than a reason for it. “Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not” (Jer 31:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lamentation as the expression of sorrow, cries of grief, the act of bewailing; to comfort as to strengthen the mind under affliction, to console; and a massacre as the slaughter of numbers with circumstances of cruelty.
webster_full: LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
COMFORT, v.t. [L. conforto, to strengthen; con and fortis, strong.] To strengthen; to invigorate; to cheer or enliven. To strengthen the mind under affliction; to console.
MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty; the indiscriminate killing of human beings, without authority or necessity.
COL'LEGE, n. A collection or assemblage; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits. An edifice appropriated to the use of students.
scriptures: Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.
Mat 2:18
In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.
Psa 13:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
Rev 6:11

And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled.
corruption_summary: The Bethlen College's Transylvanian home, burned in March 1704 with its library, its professors and its students.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the premature consolation that answers an atrocity with a doctrine before it has allowed the grief its words. Scripture quotes Rachel's refusal of comfort in the canon and does not correct her; the comfort comes, and it comes after.

The principle to recover is that lament is a sanctioned form of prayer and that the unanswered question may be asked aloud. The prophet records the refusal of comfort: “Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not” (Jer 31:15). Matthew applies the same words to a slaughter of children: “Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not” (Mat 2:18). The psalmist asks how long and receives no immediate answer: “How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?” (Psa 13:1). And the martyrs under the altar are told that the number is not yet complete: they “should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled” (Rev 6:11).

pos: n. (Transylvanian town, Romanian Turda; the Diet of 1568 that granted the first legal religious toleration in Europe)
etymology: From Hungarian Torda, of uncertain origin; Romanian Turda.
biblical_def: Torda is the town where, in January 1568, the Transylvanian Diet enacted that preachers should preach the gospel according to their own understanding, that no one should be imprisoned or deprived for his religion, and that faith is the gift of God — the first statute of its kind in Europe. It had a particular cause: Prince John Sigismund's court physician Giorgio Blandrata and his preacher Ferenc David were antitrinitarians, and the law was framed so that they could not be suppressed; the Unitarian church became one of Transylvania's four received religions. The dictionary therefore records Torda with a divided verdict. The principle that faith cannot be compelled is right, and the dictionary holds it. The judgment that the denial of Christ's deity is a thing a Christian state may receive is wrong. Both can be said, because Scripture distinguishes between tolerating a man and endorsing his doctrine: “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30) is not a verdict on the tares.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toleration as the act of tolerating, the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; harvest as the season of reaping and gathering in; and meekness as mildness and forbearance under provocation.
webster_full: TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit.
scriptures: But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.

Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
corruption_summary: The Diet of January 1568, Europe's first statute of religious toleration, framed to protect the antitrinitarians at court.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things need naming here and the dictionary names both. The corruption is the toleration that becomes endorsement: Transylvania did not merely decline to imprison the antitrinitarians, it received their church as one of the lawful religions of the realm, which is a state declaring the denial of Christ's deity to be an acceptable form of Christianity. The opposite corruption is the one Olomouc practised, belief imposed by the sword. Neither is the biblical position.

The principle to recover is that the church does not use the civil arm against error, and that the final separation is Christ's at the end. The householder forbids the premature uprooting and gives the reason: “lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them” (Mat 13:29); and the order is “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30). The Lord rebukes the disciples who wanted fire called down on the unreceptive: “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55). And the method with opponents is instruction in hope of their repentance: “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth” (2Ti 2:25).

pos: n. (Transylvanian town, Romanian Targu Mures; its Reformed college and the Teleki library)
etymology: From Hungarian Marosvasarhely, the market place on the Maros; Romanian Targu Mures.
biblical_def: Marosvasarhely kept a Reformed college from 1557 and, from 1802, the Teleki Teka, a library of some forty thousand volumes given to the town by Chancellor Samuel Teleki and open to the public — one of the first such collections in eastern Europe. The town was also where the Transylvanian Diet of 1571, after the death of the antitrinitarian prince, enacted that no further religious innovation should be introduced, which fixed the four received religions and closed the door the Diet of Torda had opened. The dictionary records the town for the library, because a Protestant culture is a reading culture and it leaves books behind. Paul's last written request was for his books, which is the most practical verse in the New Testament on this subject: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a library as a collection of books belonging to a private person or to a public institution, parchment as the skin of a sheep or goat prepared for writing, and a goad as a pointed instrument used to stimulate a beast to move faster.
webster_full: LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution.
PARCHMENT, n. The skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing.
GOAD, n. A pointed instrument used to stimulate a beast to move faster.
BOOK, n. 1. A general name of every literary composition which is printed; but appropriately, a printed composition bound.
scriptures: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
Jer 36:2

Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah, even unto this day.
And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites:
corruption_summary: A Reformed college from 1557 and the Teleki library from 1802; and the Diet of 1571 that forbade further religious innovation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion of books as a substitute for piety, which usually comes from people who have not read many. The Reformation was a movement of readers from the first week, and the towns that kept libraries kept the doctrine longest.

The principle to recover is that God's people are given written words, that they are to be kept, copied and read, and that even an apostle in prison wanted his. Paul's request is specific: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13). Words rightly taught are fixed and they prod: “The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies” (Ecc 12:11). Prophecy is to be collected into a volume: “Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee” (Jer 36:2). And a king was to make his own copy by hand: “he shall write him a copy of this law in a book” (Deu 17:18).

pos: n. (Hungarian town, Romanian Satu Mare; the synod of 1646 that settled Hungarian church government)
etymology: From Hungarian Szatmar, from a personal or tribal name; Romanian Satu Mare.
biblical_def: Szatmar was where the Hungarian Reformed church decided what kind of church it would be. Hungarian students returning from Cambridge and the Netherlands in the 1630s and 1640s brought back English Puritan divinity and with it a programme: congregational eldership, presbyterian courts in place of the bishops and seniors, stricter Sabbath observance and family discipline. The national synod held at Szatmarnemeti in June 1646, under Istvan Geleji Katona, condemned the presbyterian scheme, confirmed the superintendency, and adopted a canon law that governed the Hungarian Reformed church for centuries, while quietly taking up much of the Puritans' practical piety. The dictionary records Szatmar because the oversight of a flock is an office with a shape, and Scripture describes it in terms that rule out both lordship and neglect. “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oversight as superintendence, watchful care, the charge and management of a business; preeminence as superiority in excellence, precedence; and a burden as that which is borne, and in Scripture an oracle of weight.
webster_full: OVERSIGHT, n. Superintendence; watchful care; the charge and management of a business.
PREEMINENCE, n. Superiority in excellence; distinction in something commendable; precedence.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; and in Scripture, an oracle of weight.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district.
scriptures: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
corruption_summary: The national synod of June 1646, which condemned the Hungarian Puritans' presbyterian scheme and confirmed the superintendency.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is at both ends of the question Szatmar argued. One error makes the minister a proprietor, answerable to no court and resented for nothing because nothing is asked of him; the other multiplies courts and canons until the flock is managed and not fed. The dictionary holds the presbyterian polity the synod rejected, and still records that the synod kept much of what the Puritans wanted in practice.

The principle to recover is that oversight is pastoral feeding, willingly undertaken, without lordship. Peter states the charge and its manner: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The prohibition follows immediately: “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). Assemblies are to lay on no more than is needful: “to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things” (Act 15:28). And John names the opposite spirit in a man: “Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not” (3Jo 1:9).

“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the presbyterian scheme condemned, the superintendency kept.

pos: n. (Hungarian city, German Odenburg; the Diet of 1681 that created the articular places of Protestant worship)
etymology: From Hungarian Sopron, from a personal name Suprun; German Odenburg.
biblical_def: Sopron was where Hungarian Protestantism was given back a fraction of what had been taken. The Diet of 1681, after a decade in which hundreds of ministers had been deposed and some sent to the Neapolitan galleys, allowed Protestant worship in two designated places in each county — the articular places — and nowhere else; congregations walked many miles on a Sunday to reach them, and the wooden articular churches of Upper Hungary, built without nails or stone towers under the terms imposed, still stand. The dictionary records Sopron because a law that confines worship to appointed places is an attempt to do what the Lord told the woman of Samaria could not be done. “the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father” (Joh 4:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to worship as to pay divine honours to, to reverence with supreme respect; a temple as a building set apart for the worship of God; and a place as a particular portion of space, a locality.
webster_full: WORSHIP, v.t. To pay divine honors to; to reverence with supreme respect and veneration.
TEMPLE, n. A building set apart for the worship of God; specifically, the house built by Solomon in Jerusalem.
PLACE, n. A particular portion of space; a locality.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; the whole body of the people of Israel.
scriptures: Joh 4:21
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.
Joh 4:23
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
Act 7:48
Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet,
corruption_summary: The Diet of 1681, which allowed Protestant worship only in two articular places per county, and the wooden churches built under its terms.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the attachment of the church's life to a particular building, which a hostile state can then control by controlling the building. Hungary's Protestants were restricted to two sites in a county and walked to them; what could not be confined was the thing the law was aimed at.

The principle to recover is that acceptable worship is defined by spirit and truth and not by locality. The Lord sets the question aside: “the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father” (Joh 4:21). What God seeks is named instead: “the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him” (Joh 4:23). Paul tells the Athenians the same thing of their shrines: God “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24). And Stephen had already said it of the temple itself: “Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 7:48).
